<s>Daśabalasūtra</s> (1) 8. Furthermore, the <s>Tathāgata</s> recollects his manifold former abodes, namely: one birth, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, a hundred births, a thousand births, a hundred thousand births, many hundreds of births, many thousands of births, many hundreds of thousands of births, an aeon of dissolution, an aeon of evolution, an aeon of both dissolution and evolution, many aeons of dissolution, many aeons of evolution, many aeons of both dissolution and evolution. He recollects: 'Those beings were there where I was—of such name, such birth, such clan, such food, experiencing such pleasure and pain, of such long life, of such duration, of such life-span. Having fallen from there, I was reborn elsewhere; having fallen from there, I was reborn elsewhere; having fallen from there, I was reborn here.' Thus, with its aspects, with its causes, with its details, he recollects his manifold former abodes.

<s>Daśabalasūtra</s> (1) 9. Furthermore, the <s>Tathāgata</s>, with the divine eye, purified, surpassing human sight, sees beings dying and being reborn, beautiful and ugly, inferior and superior, going to good destinies and bad destinies, and truly knows beings as they fare according to their <s>karma</s>. 'These beings, endowed with bodily misconduct, endowed with verbal and mental misconduct, revilers of the noble ones, of wrong views, undertaking actions and laws based on wrong views—because of that cause, by that condition, upon the dissolution of the body, after death, they are reborn in states of misery, in bad destinations, in the downfall, in the hells. But these beings, endowed with good bodily conduct, endowed with good verbal and mental conduct, not revilers of the noble ones, of right views, undertaking actions and laws based on right views—because of that cause, by that condition, upon the dissolution of the body, they are reborn in a good destination, in the heavenly world, among the gods.'
